questions.q: What type of forces exist between simple discrete molecules in a molecular covalent substance?
a: Strong covalent bonds throughout the bulk solid

questions.q: Why do simple covalent substances generally have low melting and boiling points?
a: Little thermal energy is needed to overcome the weak intermolecular forces between molecules

questions.q: Why do simple covalent molecules typically fail to conduct electricity in any state?
a: They have no overall electrical charge and no mobile electrons or ions to carry current

questions.q: What is the physical state of most simple covalent substances (such as carbon dioxide, methane, and oxygen) at room temperature?
a: Gases or liquids with low boiling points

questions.q: How do the boiling points of simple covalent molecules generally change as the size and relative molecular mass of the molecules increase?
a: Boiling points increase because larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces of attraction
Boiling points decrease to absolute zero
Boiling points fluctuate randomly with no pattern

questions.q: Are simple covalent compounds generally soluble in water, and what determines their solubility?
a: Yes, all covalent compounds dissolve to form ionic solutions
Many simple covalent substances are insoluble in water unless they react with it or are polar (like ethanol), while non-polar molecules (like hexane) dissolve in organic solvents
No, covalent substances only dissolve in liquid metals
Yes, because covalent bonds break easily in water

questions.q: Which of the following substances is a simple covalent molecule that is a liquid at room temperature?

a: The strong covalent bonds holding the atoms together inside the molecule

The weak intermolecular forces between separate molecules

questions.q: Why does methane (CH4) have a much lower boiling point than water (H2O)?
a: Methane has weaker intermolecular forces between its small, non-polar molecules compared to the hydrogen bonding in water
Methane is a giant lattice structure

questions.q: Which of the following properties is characteristic of simple molecular substances?
a: Low melting and boiling points due to weak intermolecular forces

questions.q: Why do iodine crystals sublime (turn directly from a solid to a purple gas) when gently heated?
a: They melt into a liquid first
The weak intermolecular forces between iodine molecules are easily overcome by a small amount of heat energy
The covalent bonds inside the iodine molecule break

questions.q: Which of the following is a simple covalent gas at room temperature and pressure?
What happens to the volatility (tendency to turn into a gas) of simple covalent liquids as you go down a homologous series of alkanes?
a: Volatility decreases as molecular size and intermolecular forces increase

questions.q: Why do sugar (sucrose, a molecular covalent compound) solutions fail to conduct electricity?
a: When sugar dissolves, it forms separate neutral molecules in solution rather than mobile ions or electrons
Sugar molecules have a strong negative charge
Sugar reacts with the copper wires

a: Covalent intramolecular bonds are very strong, whereas intermolecular forces are relatively weak

Intermolecular forces are stronger than nuclear forces

questions.q: Why are most simple covalent compounds soft and easily scratched when in solid form (like solid wax or sulfur)?
a: Because their atoms are held by strong ionic lattices
Because little force is required to slide separate molecules past one another due to weak intermolecular forces
Because they are made of rubber

questions.q: Which of the following molecules has a triple covalent bond and makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere?
Why do some simple covalent substances dissolve well in non-polar organic solvents like petrol or methylbenzene?
a: They react chemically to form salts
They form ionic bonds with the solvent
Like dissolves like; non-polar solute molecules experience similar weak intermolecular attractions with non-polar solvent molecules

questions.q: What type of structure do most non-metal elements (other than noble gases and giant lattices like carbon) exhibit at room temperature?
a: Simple molecular structures consisting of small discrete molecules

questions.q: When liquid water boils to form steam, what physical change happens to the water molecules themselves?
a: The molecules break apart into hydrogen and oxygen atoms
The molecules remain intact, but gain enough kinetic energy to separate completely as intermolecular forces are broken
The molecules turn into ionic crystals

questions.q: Which of the following characteristics is typical of liquid simple covalent compounds like liquid bromine or ethanol?
a: Low viscosity and volatility depending on molecular weight

questions.q: Why do solid molecular substances like dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) have low enthalpy changes of vaporization?
a: Because covalent bonds require enormous energy to break
Because only weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome

questions.q: How does increasing molecular mass affect the physical state of halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine) at room temperature?
a: They transition from gases (F2, Cl2) to a liquid (Br2) to a solid (I2) as intermolecular forces strengthen with size

questions.q: Which of the following explains why hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is a gas at room temperature while water (H2O) is a liquid, despite similar molecular structures?

Hydrogen sulfide is a giant lattice
Water molecules are heavier than H2S

questions.q: What happens to the physical properties of simple molecular substances if you increase the external pressure?
a: Their melting and boiling points can change slightly, and gases can be compressed or liquefied
Their covalent bonds double in strength

questions.q: Which of the following represents a correct explanation for why ammonia (NH3) has a low melting point (-77.7°C)?
a: It is held together by a giant network of covalent bonds
It is an ionic salt crystal
It is composed of simple discrete molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces

questions.q: In terms of thermal conductivity, how do simple molecular materials generally behave?
